q-66062:
The range of $\operatorname{csc}⁡x$ consists of two intervals:

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡x\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty )
$$

Horizontal shifts and stretches have no effect on the range. Therefore,

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\in (-\infty ,-1]\cup [1,\infty ).
$$

We can split this into two inequalities:

$$
\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\le -1,\,\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\ge 1
$$

To find the range of $f(x),$ we consider both intervals separately.

- Multiplying the first interval by $5$ and subtracting $3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\le -1 \\  & 5\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\le -5 \\  & 5\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})-3\le -5-3 \\  & f(x)\le -8.\end{aligned}
$$

- Multiplying the second interval by $5$ and subtracting $3,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned} & \operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\ge 1 \\  & 5\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})\ge 5 \\  & 5\operatorname{csc}⁡(\frac{x}{4})-3\ge 5-3 \\  & f(x)\ge 2.\end{aligned}
$$

Combining both inequalities, we get

$$
f(x)\le -8,\,f(x)\ge 2.
$$

Therefore, we conclude that the range is $f(x)\in (-\infty ,-8]\cup [2,\infty ).$

q-66074:
The domain of $y=\operatorname{sec}⁡x$ consists of all values where $\operatorname{cos}⁡x\ne 0,$ and is given by the expression

$$
x\ne {90}^{∘}+n\cdot {180}^{∘},
$$

where $n$ is an integer.

To find the domain of $2\operatorname{sec}⁡(3x-{60}^{∘}),$ we replace the $x$ on the left-hand side of the above with $(3x-{60}^{∘}).$ This gives

$$
3x-{60}^{∘}\ne {90}^{∘}+n\cdot {180}^{∘}.
$$

Solving for $x,$ we get

$$
\begin{aligned}3x-{60}^{∘} & \ne {90}^{∘}+n\cdot {180}^{∘} \\ 3x & \ne {90}^{∘}+n\cdot {180}^{∘}+{60}^{∘} \\ 3x & \ne {150}^{∘}+n\cdot {180}^{∘} \\ x & \ne {50}^{∘}+n\cdot {60}^{∘}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the domain of the function is $x\ne {50}^{∘}+n\cdot {60}^{∘},$ where $n$ is an integer.

q-23799:
First, we factor the numerator:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta -\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } & =\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta (1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we rewrite the numerator using $1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta ={cos}^{2}⁡\theta $ and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta (1-{sin}^{2}⁡\theta )}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } & =\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta {cos}^{2}⁡\theta }{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta \cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }}{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }\end{aligned}
$$

Then, we rewrite $\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta $ using its definition and simplify further:

$$
\begin{aligned}\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta \cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } & =\frac{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta } \\  & =\frac{\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{2\cancel{\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta }} \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }\cdot \frac{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }}\cdot \frac{\cancel{\operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }}{2} \\  & =\frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we conclude that:

$$
\frac{\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta -\operatorname{tan}⁡\theta {sin}^{2}⁡\theta }{2\operatorname{sin}⁡\theta \operatorname{cos}⁡\theta }=\frac{1}{2}
$$

q-65231:
First, we rewrite the denominator using $1-{sin}^{2}⁡x={cos}^{2}⁡x.$

$$
\frac{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{{cos}^{2}⁡x}=\frac{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{1-{sin}^{2}⁡x}
$$

Next, we factor the denominator as difference of squares, and simplify:

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{1-{sin}^{2}⁡x} & =\frac{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}{(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)} \\  & =\frac{\cancel{1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x}}{\cancel{(1-\operatorname{sin}⁡x)}(1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x)} \\  & =\frac{1}{1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, $f(x)=1+\operatorname{sin}⁡x.$

q-31585:
If we plug in $x=0$ we get the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0},$ so  we apply L'Hopital's rule to find the limit:

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}-x-1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x-1} & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[{e}^{x}-x-1]^{′}}{[\operatorname{cos}⁡x-1]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}-1}{-\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}-1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x}\end{aligned}
$$

This time, the resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{0}{0}.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}-x-1}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x-1} & =-{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}-1}{\operatorname{sin}⁡x} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{[{e}^{x}-1]^{′}}{[\operatorname{sin}⁡x]^{′}} \\  & =-{lim}_{x\to 0}\frac{{e}^{x}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡x} \\  & =-\frac{{e}^{0}}{\operatorname{cos}⁡0} \\  & =-\frac{1}{1} \\  & =-1.\end{aligned}
$$

q-115530:
Here the limits of the numerator and denominator are ${lim}_{x\to \infty }\sqrt{x}=\infty $ and ${lim}_{x\to \infty }{ln}^{2}⁡x=\infty ,$ respectively, so we have the case $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$

Applying L'Hopital's rule, we obtain

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{ln}^{2}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{[\sqrt{x}]^{′}}{{[{ln}^{2}⁡x]}^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}})}{(\frac{2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{x}{4\sqrt{x}\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{x}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x}.\end{aligned}
$$

The resulting limit still gives the indeterminate form $\frac{\infty }{\infty }.$ To find the limit, we apply L'Hopital's rule once again. We get

$$
\begin{aligned}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{x}}{{ln}^{2}⁡x} & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{\sqrt{x}}{4\operatorname{ln}⁡x} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{[\sqrt{x}]^{′}}{[4\operatorname{ln}⁡x]^{′}} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{(\frac{1}{2\sqrt{x}})}{(\frac{4}{x})} \\  & ={lim}_{x\to \infty }\frac{x}{8\sqrt{x}} \\  & =\frac{1}{8}{lim}_{x\to \infty }\sqrt{x} \\  & =\infty .\end{aligned}
$$

q-2403:
We use the quotient rule with the numerator $u(x)=\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}$ and the denominator $v(x)=2x.$ 

Differentiating $u(x)$ and $v(x),$ we have

$$
{u}^{′}(x)=\frac{1}{2x\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}},\,{v}^{′}(x)=2.
$$

Note that we used the chain rule to differentiate $u.$

Now, applying the quotient rule and simplifying, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x} & =\frac{{u}^{′}(x)\cdot v(x)-u(x)\cdot {v}^{′}(x)}{[v(x)]^{2}} \\  & =\frac{(\frac{1}{2x\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}})(2x)-(\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x})(2)}{(2x)^{2}} \\  & =\frac{\frac{1}{\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}-2\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}{4{x}^{2}} \\  & =\frac{1-2\operatorname{ln}⁡x}{4{x}^{2}\sqrt{\operatorname{ln}⁡x}}.\end{aligned}\end{aligned}
$$
